title: A Silence for the Inventory
premise: Beatrix Brightwater, a bridge inspector who measures everything and feels nothing, returns to her estranged family home after her mother's death, where a stranger at the funeral calls the family by a name no one has ever used. Digging into her mother's hidden past, Beatrix uncovers an identity her mother buried decades ago—one entangled with a crime the law never punished and a debt of silence that shaped every Brightwater life. As her siblings fracture over what to do with the truth, Beatrix must choose between protecting the family's careful invisibility and speaking the name aloud. The novel ends at the graveside, where Beatrix finally says goodbye properly—out loud, in her mother's true name—and walks away owning herself for the first time.
about_author: Paloma Joubert is a former structural engineer from Lyon who left bridges for sentences after a decade of inspecting what holds things up. Her fiction examines the quiet architecture of families and the weight names carry across generations.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. She inspects a failing bridge while mentally measuring her marriage's cracks in millimeters, then receives the call: her mother has died. Emotional beat: numb competence as armor against grief she refuses to feel yet.

chapters.title: The House That Held Its Breath
chapters.summary: Beatrix arrives at the family home, a museum of her mother's controlled order. Her siblings Margot and Daniel orbit each other warily. POV alternates between Beatrix and Daniel. Beat: the suffocating stillness of a family that never says anything real.

chapters.title: A Stranger in Good Shoes
chapters.summary: At the funeral, an elegant older woman approaches and addresses the family by a surname nobody uses—Vasseur. She leaves before questions form. Beatrix's POV. Beat: the first fissure; invisibility revealed as something maintained, not natural.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Sorting their mother's belongings, the siblings find a locked tin box and a deed to property none of them knew existed. Daniel's POV. Beat: curiosity curdling into suspicion as the mother's curated life shows seams.

chapters.title: What Margot Remembers
chapters.summary: Margot reveals she once heard their mother on the phone, crying, saying 'I never agreed to keep it.' Beatrix dismisses it. Margot's POV. Beat: sibling rivalry resurfaces; grief expressed as accusation.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Knew
chapters.summary: Beatrix tracks down the stranger, Odile Vasseur, who admits only that she 'owed' their mother a presence at the funeral. Beatrix's POV. Beat: fascination overtaking caution; the inspector begins inspecting her own history.

chapters.title: Bridges Fail Slowly
chapters.summary: Back at work, Beatrix signs off on a compromised inspection under pressure from a powerful contractor—the novel's second corruption thread mirroring the first. Beatrix's POV. Beat: complicity; she recognizes how silence gets bought.

chapters.title: The Tin Box Opens
chapters.summary: Daniel forces the box: photographs, a newspaper clipping about a 1979 fire at a textile factory, and documents bearing the name Vasseur. Daniel's POV. Beat: dread; the family name itself becomes evidence.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Nine
chapters.summary: Through Odile, the siblings learn their mother was born Hélène Vasseur, daughter of the factory owner whose negligence killed three workers—a crime hushed up with money and a changed identity. Alternating POVs. Beat: the ground shifts; inheritance reframed as theft.

chapters.title: The Descendants of the Dead
chapters.summary: Odile reveals she is the daughter of one of the dead workers; the two families have shadowed each other for forty years. Margot's POV. Beat: shame and anger collide—Margot wants restitution, Daniel wants it buried.

chapters.title: Marriage Inspection
chapters.summary: Beatrix's husband arrives unannounced, demanding she come home; their marriage's load-bearing failures are laid bare in one brutal kitchen conversation. Beatrix's POV. Beat: she realizes she has been a tenant in her own life, like her mother was in hers.

chapters.title: Daniel's Ledger
chapters.summary: Daniel, a lawyer, calculates exposure: reputation, estate, his career. He argues the past should stay sealed. Daniel's POV. Beat: power's seduction—he begins to sound like the men who bought his grandfather's silence.

chapters.title: The Factory Floor
chapters.summary: Beatrix visits the ruined factory site and finds a memorial plaque, unofficial, nailed by someone who remembered. Beatrix's POV. Beat: grief finally arrives, displaced onto strangers' deaths; justice outside the law takes shape as an idea.

chapters.title: Blackmail, Gently Offered
chapters.summary: The contractor from Chapter 7 learns of Beatrix's family research and offers to bury both secrets together—an alliance of silences. Beatrix's POV. Beat: temptation at its most reasonable-sounding; the theme made personal.

chapters.title: Margot Breaks
chapters.summary: Margot contacts a journalist without telling anyone, detonating the family's fragile consensus. Margot's POV. Beat: righteous fury shadowed by guilt; the first irreversible act.

chapters.title: The Name in Print
chapters.summary: The story runs; the Vasseur name and the Brightwater alias appear side by side. Daniel threatens to cut Margot off entirely. Alternating POVs. Beat: the family shatters along its oldest fault lines.

chapters.title: Odile's Testimony
chapters.summary: Odile shares her mother's letters—evidence enough to reopen the case, but she asks not for money, only for the name spoken publicly by those who carried it. Odile's POV (first time). Beat: grace offered where retribution was expected.

chapters.title: What Beatrix Signs
chapters.summary: Beatrix refuses the contractor's deal and files a truthful amended inspection report, ending her career's quiet complicity. Beatrix's POV. Beat: climax of the personal thread—she chooses ownership over tenancy.

chapters.title: Reckoning at the Table
chapters.summary: The siblings confront each other and their mother's memory around the dinner table; Daniel's collapse into tears reveals his fear was always abandonment, not scandal. All three POVs interwoven. Beat: emotional climax; truth spoken aloud at last.

chapters.title: Hélène
chapters.summary: The reopened inquiry vindicates the workers' families; the estate funds a proper memorial. Daniel, transformed, handles the legal restoration of the true name himself. Daniel's POV. Beat: justice achieved—not vengeance, but acknowledgment.

chapters.title: A Silence, Properly Ended
chapters.summary: At the graveside, Beatrix speaks the eulogy her mother never had, naming her Hélène Vasseur Brightwater aloud before witnesses, including Odile. Beatrix's POV. Beat: catharsis; goodbye said properly, out loud, before the memory went entirely.

chapters.title: Owner, Not Tenant
chapters.summary: Months later: Beatrix divorced, rehired as an independent inspector, walking a new bridge she certified honestly. She signs her own full name to the report. Beatrix's POV. Beat: resolution—identity claimed, silence ended, the structure holding.
